newsitem.title: FINLAND: POSCO head expects higher steel prices.
newsitem.headline: POSCO head expects higher steel prices.

text.p: South Korean Pohang Iron & Steel Co Ltd (POSCO) -- aiming to be the biggest steel group in the world in 1999 -- expects steel prices to improve soon, POSCO chairman Kim Mahn-ja said on Monday.

"I think we have hit the bottom. We expect prices to improve in the coming months," he told a Reuters reporter at the opening day of the annual congress of the International Iron and Steel Institute (IISI) here.
"In the U.S., prices have been recovering ahead of other markets (and) Europe is following suit," Kim said.
"Prices in Japan are rising slowly, and we hope Korea will follow," he added.
On September 13, POSCO forecast its calendar 1996 profit would fall to 640 billion won from 840 billion in 1995.
"If we get to that figure (640 billion won) we think we will be doing well," Kim said on Monday.
"Profits in the manufacturing industry in Korea have been dropping fast," he said.
Due to the recent depreciation of the external value of the won, "our input costs and foreign debt will rise," he added.
Looking to next year, Kim said: "I hope we can rebound our profit level in 1997 because we will have bigger capacity in stainless steel."
On August 30, POSCO said it had doubled its stainless steel production to 840,000 tonnes per year.
Kim repeated POSCO's target to raise steel output to 26 million tonnes in 1997 from 24 million this year and 23 million in 1995, noting: "We are steadily increasing".

He also repeated POSCO's aim to be the world's biggest steel producer in 1999. The group has said it is aiming at a steel products output of 28 million tonnes in 1999. It is currently the world number two steelmaker.
Asked about new investments or acquisitions, Kim said POSCO was already "big enough". He added: "We would like to have some more downstream production", but did not elaborate.
Taking a long-term view, the POSCO chairman said energy -- which the group has said is expected to generate three percent of turnover in 2005 -- would be an important cash-generating supplement.
Energy would "provide a steady flow of income which would be good for a steel producer," he said.
